 By Orlando Sentinel Editorial Board | insight@orlandosentinel.com and Sun Sentinel Editorial Board | Sun Sentinel PUBLISHED: October 29, 2026 at 6:30 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... As you fill out your ballot, tune out the candidates’ rhetoric. Consider the facts. Regardless of your party, there are questions to which you deserve answers.
 What have candidates actually done to prove they’re on your side? Have they fought for people like you? Or did they climb the political ladder by scapegoating those who can’t fight back?
 If they have held office, did they keep their promises to help people? Or did they favor the wealthy interests that financed their campaigns? Did they faithfully fulfill their duties? How many times did they get caught lying?
 In the two statewide races for powerful Cabinet offices, the reality is not pretty.
 Long before Gov. Ron DeSantis promoted James Uthmeier from his chief of staff to state attorney general, and elevated state Sen. Blaise Ingoglia to chief financial officer, both offered reasons for concern.
 A schemer for DeSantis
 Uthmeier is the dark architect of many of DeSantis’ most reprehensible schemes, including taking money meant for state use to fly asylum-seekers from Texas to Martha’s Vineyard.
 He was neck-deep in a scheme that swiped $10 million that should have gone to Medicaid and was diverted through the nonprofit Hope Florida Foundation and eventually to political campaigns. And scant public records around the outrageous boondoggle that poured more than $1 billion into a hellhole immigration detention camp in the Everglades point to him as the key engineer.
 As attorney general, he arrogantly declares laws he doesn’t like to be “unconstitutional,” including a post-Parkland age limit on firearm purchases; sensible growth boundaries; and a public mandate for fair legislative districts. Similar laws have passed constitutionality tests in other states and even in Florida, but he values his own opinion above everyone else’s.
 Floridians have a far better option here. José Javier Rodríguez has worked hard to defend those needing help, as a pro-consumer state senator from Miami-Dade and as a federal labor official.
 Like Uthmeier, Ingoglia is a product of pure Capitol cronyism. He was appointed, not elected.
 An Amendment 3 propagandist
 The best we can say about him is that Ingoglia’s shenanigans aren’t as blatant as Uthmeier’s, but the deception he has practiced as CFO might do more long-term damage to our cities and counties.
 Soon after DeSantis appointed Ingoglia, he barnstormed the state, hoping to convince Floridians that local spending was out of control, while ignoring state spending abuses.
 He launched phony audits of local governments, using a cockeyed formula that he claimed proved that spending was out of control and citing inaccurate numbers.
 If Ingoglia really wanted to point out wasteful spending, he should have done just that. We can only assume he couldn’t find many juicy examples — because local governments, for the most part, are held far more accountable for the money they budget, including a requirement to go to voters before taking on substantial debt.
 Ingoglia’s dog-and-phony show served less noble goals.
 State lawmakers cited his antics as the legitimate basis for Amendment 3, which would eliminate non-school property taxes for Florida homeowners.
 Another viable Democratic option
 The bottom line: Amendment 3 is not really a tax cut but a tax shift with massive unforeseen consequences that could blow up in everyone’s faces, including homeowners who supposedly would benefit. If it passes, Ingoglia will largely be to blame for building the foundation of lies that supported it.
 Here, too, Florida voters have a worthy alternative in Annette Taddeo, a seasoned leader and small business owner who served in the state Senate, where she worked to defend the first responders who might lose their jobs if Amendment 3 passes.
 Look at both races. It should be clear that this is not a partisan issue.
 Republicans hate being lied to as much as Democrats do. Nonpartisan voters are just as disgusted by politicians who sacrifice the public good for their personal gain. And voters should be incensed when state officials take it upon themselves to ignore the will of the people, as expressed through local elections.
 Uthmeier and Ingoglia are standing before the very same voters they repeatedly undermined and deceived, pretending to be accomplished incumbents.
 All over Florida, voters are saying that they want change. Here’s a good place to start. These are two of the easiest choices on the Florida ballot.
 The Sun Sentinel Editorial Board consists of Opinion Editor Steve Bousquet, Deputy Opinion Editor Dan Sweeney, editorial writers Pat Beall and Martin Dyckman and Executive Editor Gretchen Day-Bryant. Contact us by email at letters@sun-sentinel.com .
